item.text: {"question_id":"4B.3","answer":"In 2023, formal protections and some limited corrective actions coexisted with broad, recurring restrictions on opposition, criticism, satire, journalism, protest, association, and civil-society activity. The revised press law guaranteed access to some non-classified public-interest information, but retained important security-related exclusions and did not explicitly abolish prison sentences for press offenses. [BATCH-0025-E007] Authorities sometimes released detainees, arrested some officers, condemned abuses, or promised accountability: Franck Diongo was released without charge; three officers were arrested after the May protest; journalists detained in several incidents were released, in some cases after UN intervention; the government condemned attacks and promised justice; and Tshisekedi said he would not intervene in the Bujakera case, invoking separation of powers. These steps show partial response, but not consistent protection or effective remedy, because final findings, sanctions, and independent accountability were generally unestablished. [BATCH-0002-E012, BATCH-0003-E007, BATCH-0025-E011, BATCH-0025-E013, BATCH-0026-E007, BATCH-0026-E011, BATCH-0027-E005, BATCH-0011-E021] Direct adverse evidence includes the violent dispersal of the May opposition march, blocked opposition meetings and demonstrations, arrests and searches involving opposition figures, and rhetoric by Tshisekedi asserting that criticism about rights violations or deprivation of freedoms would not change his security posture. [BATCH-0002-E011, BATCH-0003-E002, BATCH-0003-E007, BATCH-0003-E010] Journalists and critics were detained or prosecuted over reporting, criticism, alleged false information, or satire, including the arrests of Shilo FM journalists, Gustave Bakuka, Diègo Kayiba, John Ngongo Lomango, satirical comedian Junior Nkole, Lens Omelonga, and Stanis Bujakera; soldiers also arrested and beat three journalists covering a land dispute. [BATCH-0025-E011, BATCH-0025-E012, BATCH-0026-E007, BATCH-0026-E011, BATCH-0010-E013] Election-related journalists and opposition participants faced violence from suspected ruling-party or allied supporters, including the alleged assault by an MLC leader and militants, attacks on journalists and an opposition candidate in Kananga, and a broadcast environment marked by threats and pressure. Government condemnation and promised prosecution were reported in one case, but the supplied record does not establish completed accountability. [BATCH-0027-E004, BATCH-0027-E005, BATCH-0003-E010] Human-rights defenders were also the subjects of OHCHR communications concerning alleged assassination, intrusion, threats, and intimidation; these records establish allegations requiring caution, not proven presidential responsibility or final findings. [BATCH-0021-E010, BATCH-0021-E011] The Goma operation against a banned demonstration was especially severe: security forces killed at least 56 people according to the official count, with a higher UN estimate, injured many, arrested more than 150, detained and mistreated civilians, and prosecuted many survivors through proceedings Amnesty found materially flawed. Some security personnel were convicted and reparations were ordered, but investigations were incomplete, victims and witnesses faced procedural barriers, higher-level responsibility was not fully examined, and many families lacked information or effective remedy. [BATCH-0011-E018, BATCH-0011-E020, BATCH-0011-E021] A peaceful October youth protest was reportedly escorted by police and its memorandum received, showing that civic space was not uniformly closed; however, this isolated event does not outweigh the broader pattern. [BATCH-0022-E014] Most incidents are attributed to state agencies, security forces, regulators, provincial officials, or party supporters rather than to a proven personal presidential order. Tshisekedi's direct public praise for the police chief after the May crackdown is nevertheless an adverse ruler-attribution signal, while his public statements favoring equality and institutional cooperation are rhetoric rather than proof of protection in practice.
